context_blurb:
How do you test a claim that sincere people believe? Honest people can fool themselves, and others, without meaning to. Three famous tests show two guards that keep a test fair: hiding what could sway the result from the people involved, and fixing a pass mark before testing.

In Paris the German physician Franz Mesmer taught that an invisible fluid flows through all living things, that illness comes when its flow is blocked, and that a healer can set it flowing again: animal magnetism. His patients often fell into fits, which he held were healing. In 1784 a commission headed by Benjamin Franklin tested the claim on patients of Mesmer's follower Charles d'Eslon, since Mesmer refused to take part.

The chemist Antoine Lavoisier designed trials to pull apart the two possible causes of the fits, the fluid and the patients' belief. Some patients were magnetised in secret; others only thought they were. If the fluid were real, the secret treatment would bring on fits; if belief were the cause, the pretend one would. Blindfolds and screens kept the patients from knowing, so their expectations could not sway the result, which makes these among the first blind tests on record.

One woman sat blindfolded, assured that d'Eslon was at work on her though he was nowhere near, and fell into a fit within about three minutes. Another, truly magnetised through a paper screen for thirty minutes without knowing it, showed nothing. Only the woman who believed she was being treated had a fit. The fit was real; its cause was expecting a treatment, not the treatment itself, an effect now called a placebo effect.

In Berlin, a retired mathematics teacher, Wilhelm von Osten, sincerely believed his horse Hans could do arithmetic, spell and read a clock, tapping out answers with a hoof, and charged nothing to watch. In 1904 a panel of thirteen, led by the psychologist Carl Stumpf, found no tricks. The panel was right that nobody cheated, for Hans did as well for strangers as for his owner, yet the horse was not counting: ruling out cheating had left the real question open.

Stumpf's assistant Oskar Pfungst kept testing, changing one thing at a time. Hans failed only when the person asking did not know the answer himself, or stood where the horse could not see him. Hans was right 98 times in 100 for a questioner who knew the number, and 8 for one who did not. Pfungst watched the questioners grow tense as Hans tapped. At the right count the questioner relaxed and his head jerked upward a tiny bit, about a millimetre by one account, and Hans stopped on that signal.

Taking the questioner's place himself, Pfungst gave Hans the cue without meaning to, though he knew exactly what it was. No one can simply decide not to give a cue, so a fair test keeps the answer from the questioner, or the questioner out of sight. The trap is now called the Clever Hans effect.

Therapeutic touch is a nursing practice from the 1970s: practitioners hold their hands near a patient to sense and adjust what they call the human energy field. In 1996 nine-year-old Emily Rosa tested it for her school science fair. Each practitioner slid both arms under a tall screen, out of sight; a coin toss picked one hand, Emily hovered her own hand over it, and the practitioner named the hand. Each had described feeling the field, as tingling, heat or cold.

In 280 tries the 21 practitioners found the right hand 123 times, or 44 percent. Pure guessing would be right about half the time, some 140 times, so the authors called the score close to what chance would give: no sign of any sense at all. A true ability, they noted, should have found her hand every time.

The pass mark, fixed before any trial, was at least 8 right in 10, far above the 5 that guessing gives on average, because guessing alone often reaches 6 or 7: it gets 6 or more over a third of the time. Luck reaches 8 only about once in 18 tries. Fixed in advance, the mark could not be moved to fit the scores once they were in.

Practice made no clear difference either: the practitioners had from one to twenty-seven years of it, and the authors found no clear link between their years and their scores.
